lesson.title: Why Copper Sulfate Is Blue: Light, Electrons, and the Color of Solutions
lesson.summary: Many aqueous solutions, especially those of transition metal ions, are colored because their electrons absorb specific-energy photons of visible light, and the color the eye perceives is roughly the complement of whatever wavelengths were absorbed.
lesson.body:
Recall that a solution is a homogeneous mixture in which solute particles, here specifically dissolved ions, are spread evenly throughout a solvent, and that the electromagnetic spectrum places visible light in a narrow band from about 400 to 700 nanometers, with each wavelength corresponding to a specific photon energy through E = hc/lambda, where shorter wavelengths carry higher energy. Some ionic solutions, like NaCl(aq) or KNO3(aq), are perfectly colorless, while others, like CuSO4(aq), which is blue, KMnO4(aq), which is deep purple, and NiCl2(aq), which is green, are vividly colored. The difference comes down to electron structure.

Color in solution arises mainly from ions, especially many transition metal ions, that have partially filled d electron orbitals. When such an ion is surrounded by water molecules or other ligands in solution, its d orbitals split into slightly different energy levels rather than staying identical to one another. An electron can then absorb a photon of just the right energy to jump from the lower-energy set of d orbitals to the higher-energy set, a process called a d to d transition. Ions with completely empty or completely full sets of d orbitals, such as Na+, K+, or Zn2+, have no available d to d transition that matches a visible-light photon energy, which is exactly why their solutions are colorless.

White light contains all visible wavelengths mixed together. When a solution selectively absorbs a particular band of that light, the wavelengths that are not absorbed continue on to reach your eye, and the mixture of what remains is perceived as a color that is roughly the complement, on the color wheel, of whatever was absorbed.

Here is a worked example using the pale blue color of hydrated copper(II) ion. The complex ion Cu(H2O)6 2+ has a broad d to d absorption band centered around 800 nanometers, right at the red edge of the visible spectrum bordering the near infrared. Because it absorbs mostly in the red region, the light that passes through or is reflected back to your eye is relatively enriched in blue and cyan wavelengths, which is why copper(II) sulfate solutions look pale blue. The energy of one absorbed photon at 800 nm can be found from E = hc/lambda, using h = 6.626 times 10 to the negative 34 J s, c = 3.00 times 10 to the 8 m/s, and lambda = 8.00 times 10 to the negative 7 m: E = (6.626 times 10 to the negative 34)(3.00 times 10 to the 8) divided by (8.00 times 10 to the negative 7), which equals 2.48 times 10 to the negative 19 J per photon. Multiplying by Avogadro's number, 6.022 times 10 to the 23 per mole, gives the energy per mole of photons: 2.48 times 10 to the negative 19 J times 6.022 times 10 to the 23 per mol equals about 1.50 times 10 to the 5 J/mol, or roughly 150 kJ/mol.

That is a comparatively modest amount of energy, well below the several hundred kilojoules per mole typically needed to break a covalent bond, and it is exactly why d to d transitions correspond to visible or near-infrared light rather than the far more energetic ultraviolet photons needed for many other electronic transitions. It is worth noting that this same principle, a solution's characteristic and reproducible absorption of light, is what makes the serial dilutions from earlier in this unit so useful in practice: diluting a colored solution to several precisely known concentrations and measuring how much light each one absorbs is exactly how a calibration curve is built in colorimetry and spectrophotometry.
